stem: A worker's annual money wage and the consumer price index (base 2019 = 100) are: 2019 wage Rs 24000, CPI 100; 2020 wage Rs 26000, CPI 110; 2021 wage Rs 28000, CPI 125; 2022 wage Rs 31000, CPI 145; 2023 wage Rs 33000, CPI 150. In which year was the worker's real wage (purchasing power) the lowest?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Deflate each wage: real = money wage / CPI * 100. That gives 24000, 23636, 22400, 21379, 22000 for 2019 to 2023. The minimum is 21379 in 2022; real wage falls through 2022 then recovers in 2023 because the 2023 raise outran the small CPI rise from 145 to 150.

Picks 2023 because its CPI is highest, assuming the dearest year must have the lowest real wage. But real wage also depends on the money wage; in 2023 CPI rose only 145 to 150 while the wage jumped 31000 to 33000, so real wage rose to 22000, above 2022.
Picks 2019 as the year of the smallest money wage, equating lowest nominal wage with lowest purchasing power. With CPI = 100 the 2019 real wage is 24000, in fact the highest of all five years.
Picks 2021, whose real wage 22400 is low but not the minimum. Stopping before deflating 2022 misses that the 2022 real wage 21379 is lower still.

explanation: Real wage = money wage / CPI * 100. The five real wages are 24000, 23636, 22400, 21379, 22000. The trough is 21379 in 2022, after which the 2023 wage rise of 2000 against a CPI rise of only 5 points lifts real wage back to 22000. The nominal series rises every year, so only deflation reveals the dip.

explanation_sections.punchline: A money wage that rises every year can still buy less; the trough of the real series need not be the last year or the dearest year. Deflate all five before judging.
explanation_sections.approach: Convert every nominal figure to real terms with real = nominal / price index * 100, then compare the real series. Do not infer the trough from the price index alone or from the nominal series alone.
explanation_sections.lesson: Real value = nominal value / price index * 100; purchasing power depends on both the wage and the price level, not either one by itself.
explanation_sections.timing: About 170 seconds. The fastest elimination is 2023, the highest-CPI trap: its small price rise is outpaced by the wage rise, so its real wage is not the lowest.
